newsitem.title: USA: Dollar finishes lower in U.S., below 1.70 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finishes lower in U.S., below 1.70 marks.

text.p: The dollar closed lower against most major currencies, pressured by comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer and the release of a Federal Reserve survey on the U.S. economy, experts said.
While the Tietmeyer comments did cause the dollar to slide versus the mark, traders and analysts also attributed the decline to the German currency's sharp gains versus the yen.

Speaking after a Franco-German summit in Lyon, France, Tietmeyer repeated his opposition to further gains in the dollar versus the mark. He emphasized that Germany remains interested in a "stable" mark.
Since the dollar slid to a post-World War II low of 1.3438 marks on March 8, 1995, it has risen some 28 percent versus the German currency.
"(Tietmeyer is) basically trying to say that he believes that the dollar has corrected against the deutschemark," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group.
The dollar's fall on Wednesday also accelerated when previously set orders to sell were triggered after the currency tumbled below 1.70 marks.
The greenback ended at 1.6925/30 marks and 122.15/25 yen, down from 1.7036/39 marks and 122.50/60 yen at the open.
The dollar had posted gains versus the yen early in the session.

The yield on the benchmark 182nd 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) fell on Wednesday to a record low of 2.295 percent as the price shot higher. Yields on JGBs are much lower than yields on comparable bonds of countries such as Canada, Germany, the U.S., Australia and New Zealand.
John Rothfield, an international economist at Nationsbanc, noted that Japanese bond yields are not very attractive.
"So, it encourages capital to flow out of Japan, which weakens the yen (and) helps the dollar," Rothfield said.
Yet the dollar deepened its losses after the Fed survey, called the "Beige Book," showed the U.S. economy continues to plow ahead with little sign of inflationary pressures.

The survey said price increases at retailers and manufacturers were generally temperate, partly because stiff competition made it hard to boost prices. In some areas, rising productivity was offsetting higher costs for wages and raw materials, it said.
Fed policymakers will use this information when they meet on March 25 to consider whether to raise short-term interest rates for the first time in over two years.

"People are reading in the Fed will not raise with these comments and with the Beige Book, but I don't think that's going to be the case," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
"But that is what they're reading into it (and) definitely why they're selling (dollars)," he added.
Elsewhere, the mark traded near 72.17 yen late in the session, up from 71.88/91 in very early dealings.
The dollar ended at 1.4545/55 Swiss francs, down sharply from 1.4700/10 francs at the open.
Sterling rose to $1.5988/98 from $1.5920/30.
The dollar also slid to Canadian $1.3627/32 from C$1.3673/78.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7951/56, up from $0.7940/45.
